chapter: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
title: Norman Granz and George Wein as real supporters of jazz
summary: Wilson credits Granz's touring troupes and Wein's Newport and world festivals, recalling a Piper Cub flight to Newport with Billie Holiday.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Norman Granz paid good money to his musicians; he's made a fortune, and he helped spread jazz around, too, don't you think -- during those years in the late forties and early fifties when the big bands all started falling apart.
Those little troops with Dizzy and Roy and starting out with Nat Cole and Oscar Peterson later and then Ella and Flip Phillips, Jo Jones, Gene Krupa
and Buddy Rich. Ray Brown. That carried the banner of jazz all over the world. They made a tremendous [impression], in Europe and Japan.

So you got to give Norman GranZ some credit. But I would say those three -- Norman GranZ and George Wein started his festival, the Newport Festival of 1954, and now he's presented jazz all over the world. I worked with George all over South America, Vienna, Spain, France, Holland, all over Europe -- New Orleans, etc.
I played with you at Newport once.
At Newport, yeah. Billie Holiday was up there, too. Jo Jones. Gerry Mulligan, Lester Young.
Sure, we were there with Billie Holiday. Do you remember that plane we flew up in?
Oh sure, that little Piper Cub.

Yeah. But those three fellows, to me, you have to take them into account seriously. But a lot of the other people in the jazz movement, the writers and people who -- agents, and those who make money out of it all, are more parasites, they don't do any good at all. They do more harm than good, some of them do.
